newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Khmer Rouge fighting in Cambodia remains cloudy.
newsitem.headline: Khmer Rouge fighting in Cambodia remains cloudy.

text.p: Pol Pot and his surrounded remnant of followers are apparently still holding out against opponents from within the unravelling Khmer Rouge army but details reaching Phnom Penh are sketchy, military officials said on Sunday.

As government commanders tried to assess the Khmer Rouge's latest, and possibly last, internal struggle in the thick jungle of northern Cambodia, talk in the capital turned to the political future of the less despised members of the guerrilla movement -- an issue which sharply divides the country's mis-matched coalition government.

While it seems inconceivable to many that the hated guerrillas responsible for the 1975-1979 "killing fields" regime could win a place in mainstream politics, that prospect is increasingly likely, officials and analysts said.
"I don't think this is the end of the Khmer Rouge at all," parliamentarian Son Chhay told Reuters.
"They're abandoning their fighting, but they're moving on to political struggle," he said.
Just where the fighting stood was unclear.

The remote area of the reported fighting and conflicting reports from the government's two main political factions have made it difficult to determine the status of the battle or the fate of Pol Pot, one of the 20th Century's most infamous political leaders.
"We have not been informed of any new developments," senior military adviser Tom Sombol told Reuters.
He said several senior military officials have been sent to the northern provincial town of Siem Reap, about 125 km (75 miles) from Pol Pot's reported location.
On Sunday evening, several senior officials told Reuters they believed fighting was continuing but had no new details.
On Saturday senior military officials said 1,000 rebels who have broken with Pol Pot had surrounded his position about 20 km (12 miles) east of his northern stronghold of Anlong Veng.
They reported sporadic fighting had taken place among the divided Khmer Rouge guerrillas in the rough jungle terrain.
Deputy chief of general staff Nhiek Bun Chhay said Pol Pot was holding at least three senior Khmer Rouge officials as hostages.

Pol Pot fled Anlong Veng after slaughtering his defence chief Son Sen and 11 of his family, Nhiek Bun Chhay said. He showed grisly photos of crumpled bodies he identified as Son Sen, his wife Yun Yat and their family.

While there is consensus in Phnom Penh that the rebels have split and are fighting each other, many analysts and Second Prime Minister Hun Sen expressed doubt over the reports that Pol Pot had taken top comrades, including the rebel government's president Khieu Samphan, as hostages.
An aide to former Khmer Rouge foreign minister Ieng Sary, who broke with Pol Pot last August, told Reuters he also did not believe the reports and would not help fight the rebels.
But First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh told reporters on Friday that he believed Khieu Samphan was a hostage.
The problem of conflicting reports from the two leaders, who formed a strained coalition government after U.N.-sponsored elections in 1993, is not unusual.

Ranariddh and Hun Sen have been competing to recruit rebels to their respective sides since the Khmer Rouge began unravelling last August, and analysts said they typically produce information that serves their individual agendas.

Ranariddh is eager to make peace with the guerrillas and forge a planned political alliance with Khieu Samphan, but Hun Sen said on Saturday he wants to let the Khmer Rouge fight it out among themselves.

Reports that Khieu Samphan is a hostage are thought to benefit Ranariddh by making the rebel president appear more moderate than Pol Pot and more palatable to Cambodian voters, who will have to decide between the two leaders' parties in elections next year.
More than one million Cambodians died during the Khmer Rouge's brutal 1975-79 rule through executions, starvation, disease and overwork.
In interviews on Sunday, a cross-section of Cambodians said the only thing they knew for sure was that Pol Pot deserves to die.
